days.title: The Cell Cycle & Its Control Points
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the phases of the cell cycle.
  • Identify the three major checkpoints.
  • Explain the importance of checkpoints.
  • Relate cell cycle failure to disease.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Cell cycle — the series of stages a cell goes through to divide.
  • Interphase — G1, S, G2 phases (90% of cycle).
  • M phase — mitosis + cytokinesis.
  • Checkpoint — a control point that ensures accuracy.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Phases of the Cell Cycle

PhaseWhat Happens
G1Cell grows, carries out normal functions
SDNA replication
G2Further growth; prepares for division
M (mitosis)Nuclear division: prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase
CytokinesisDivision of cytoplasm

B. Control Points (Checkpoints)

  • G1 checkpoint — checks size, nutrients, DNA damage. If failed, cell exits cycle (G0).
  • G2 checkpoint — confirms DNA replication complete and undamaged.
  • M checkpoint — ensures chromosomes are properly attached to spindle fibers.

C. When Checkpoints Fail

Uncontrolled cell division → cancer. Mutations in checkpoint genes (e.g., p53) allow damaged cells to keep dividing.

scenarios.text: The cell is replicating its DNA.
The cell is growing and carrying out normal functions.
The cell is checking that DNA replication is complete.
The cell is dividing its nucleus.
The cell has stopped dividing and entered G0.
Chromosomes are being checked for proper spindle attachment.

questions.text: During which phase does DNA replication occur?
What happens if the G1 checkpoint fails?
Which of the following would result from failure of cell cycle control?

takeaways: The cell cycle has four main stages: G1, S, G2, M.
Interphase is the longest part, occupying ~90% of the cycle.
Failure of checkpoints can lead to cancer.

days.title: Mitosis: Stages & Significance
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the stages of mitosis.
  • Explain what happens to chromosomes in each stage.
  • Identify the significance of mitosis.
  • Explain cytokinesis in plant vs animal cells.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Mitosis — division producing two genetically identical daughter cells.
  • Chromatid — one half of a duplicated chromosome.
  • Centromere — the point where sister chromatids are joined.
  • Cytokinesis — division of cytoplasm.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Stages of Mitosis (PMAT)

StageWhat Happens
ProphaseChromatin condenses into chromosomes; nuclear envelope breaks down; spindle fibers form
MetaphaseChromosomes align at the cell's equator (metaphase plate)
AnaphaseSister chromatids separate; move to opposite poles
TelophaseNuclear envelopes reform; chromosomes decondense; cytokinesis begins

B. Significance of Mitosis

  • Growth
  • Repair and healing
  • Asexual reproduction (in some organisms)
  • Maintains chromosome number (diploid → diploid)

C. Cytokinesis

  • Animal cells: Cleavage furrow pinches cell in two
  • Plant cells: Cell plate forms between the two nuclei

scenarios.text: Chromosomes line up at the cell's center.
Sister chromatids move to opposite poles.
Chromatin condenses; nuclear envelope breaks down.
Two new nuclear envelopes form.
A cleavage furrow appears in an animal cell.
A cell plate forms in a plant cell.

questions.text: During which stage do chromosomes align at the equator?
What is the main significance of mitosis?
How does cytokinesis differ in plant vs animal cells?

choices.label: Animal: cleavage furrow; Plant: cell plate

takeaways: Mitosis has four stages: Prophase, Metaphase, Anaphase, Telophase (PMAT).
It produces two genetically identical diploid cells.
Mitosis is for growth, repair, and asexual reproduction.
Cytokinesis differs: cleavage furrow (animal) vs cell plate (plant).

days.title: Meiosis: Stages & Crossing Over
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Describe the stages of meiosis.
  • Explain crossing over and recombination.
  • Differentiate mitosis from meiosis.
  • Explain how meiosis generates genetic diversity.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Meiosis — reduction division producing four haploid cells.
  • Homologous chromosomes — pairs of chromosomes (one from each parent).
  • Crossing over — exchange of segments between homologs.
  • Chiasma — the point of crossing over.

📚 Lesson Content

A. Two Rounds of Division

StageKey Event
Prophase IHomologs pair (synapsis); crossing over occurs
Metaphase IHomolog pairs line up at equator
Anaphase IHomologs separate (not sister chromatids)
Telophase ITwo haploid cells formed
Meiosis IISister chromatids separate — like mitosis

B. Crossing Over

During Prophase I, homologous chromosomes exchange segments at chiasmata. This creates new allele combinations, generating genetic diversity.

C. Mitosis vs Meiosis

AspectMitosisMeiosis
PurposeGrowth, repairGametes
Divisions12
Daughter cells2 (diploid)4 (haploid)
Genetic diversityNoYes
Crossing overNoYes

scenarios.text: Produces two genetically identical cells.
Produces four haploid cells.
Crossing over occurs.
Used for growth and repair.
Reduces chromosome number by half.
Produces gametes.

questions.text: During which stage of meiosis does crossing over occur?
How many daughter cells are produced at the end of meiosis?
What is the significance of crossing over?

takeaways: Meiosis is a two-round division producing four haploid cells.
Crossing over in Prophase I generates genetic diversity.
Homologs separate in Anaphase I; sister chromatids in Anaphase II.
Mitosis produces identical cells; meiosis produces diverse gametes.

days.title: Applications & Cell Cycle Disorders
days.content:
🎯 Learning Objectives

  • Explain applications of mitosis and meiosis.
  • Identify disorders caused by cell cycle malfunction.
  • Describe how cancer develops.
  • Explain nondisjunction and its effects.

🔑 Key Concepts

  • Nondisjunction — failure of chromosomes to separate properly.
  • Aneuploidy — abnormal chromosome number.
  • Oncogene — gene that promotes cancer.
  • Tumor suppressor gene — gene that prevents cancer (e.g., p53).

📚 Lesson Content

A. Applications of Mitosis

  • Wound healing and tissue repair
  • Asexual reproduction in plants (cuttings, grafting)
  • Cloning
  • Cancer research (studying uncontrolled division)

B. Applications of Meiosis

  • Gamete production (sperm/egg)
  • Genetic diversity in offspring
  • Selective breeding
  • Understanding genetic disorders

C. Cell Cycle Disorders

DisorderCause
CancerUncontrolled cell division
Down syndromeTrisomy 21 (nondisjunction)
Turner syndromeMonosomy X
Klinefelter syndromeXXY

scenarios.text: A cut on your skin heals.
Sperm cells are produced.
A plant grows from a cutting.
Genetic diversity is generated in offspring.
A tumor forms from uncontrolled division.
A zygote has an extra chromosome 21.

questions.text: Which application is specific to mitosis?
What is a tumor suppressor gene?

choices.label: A gene that prevents uncontrolled division

takeaways: Mitosis is applied in healing, asexual reproduction, and cloning.
Meiosis is applied in gamete production, diversity, and breeding.
Nondisjunction leads to aneuploidy (e.g., Down syndrome).
Cancer results from mutations in cell cycle control genes.
